title: The Macrophage Niche as a Primary Oncogenic Architect: A Two-Hit Systems Biology Hypothesis
content: Traditional oncology treats cell-intrinsic somatic mutations as absolute cancer initiators, viewing the immune microenvironment merely as a late-stage promoter. This paper introduces the Two-Hit Systems Biology Model, inverting this framework by proposing that oncogenesis begins with a primary genetic, epigenetic, or functional malfunction within Tissue-Resident Macrophages (TRMs)—constituting Hit 1 (The Permissive Soil). This establishes a localized cellular blind spot. Malignant transformation occurs when a subsequent driver mutation strikes an adjacent parenchymal cell: Hit 2 (The Somatic Seed). Hit 2 can be endogenously engineered via an Autonomous ROS Bridge (Pathway A), where sub-lethal, smoldering TRM-derived oxidative stress drives somatic transversions across an ultra-localized synapse, or acquired via an Exogenous Parallel Pathway (Pathway B). The pre-corrupted niche actively shields and amplifies Hit 2, explaining the rapid onset of embryonic-derived pediatric tumors. To intercept this axis, I detail early-detection protocols leveraging systemic proxies—including myeloid exosomal cargo profiling and clonal monocyte tracking—paired with targeted therapeutic interventions via NOX inhibitors and LNP-mediated M1-like state repolarization. Finally, I propose a dual-recombinase in vivo validation strategy and map this architecture across 16 human tissues.
